growth_story.headline: Honduras grows slowly but steadily, carried by money sent home by migrants and knocked back again and again by storms and crises.
growth_story.arc: Since 1990 Honduras's growth has run in three eras, each slower than the one before. The data show income per person rising 17.7 percent a year from 1990 to 1997, a pace the sources do not describe; the World Bank says Hurricane Mitch in 1998 abruptly ended a period of expansion. From 1998 to 2007 growth averaged 4.2 percent a year; in these years the country joined the CAFTA-DR trade agreement, and after Mitch Hondurans began moving to the United States in large numbers. Since 2008 it has averaged 1.2 percent: the 2009 global financial crisis, made worse by a political crisis at home, cut income per person by 4.5 percent, and the pandemic and hurricanes Eta and Iota cut it by 10.5 percent in 2020. Growth since then has been steady but moderate, 1.6 percent a year over 2016–2025 against 1.4 in the decade before, carried mostly by household spending paid for by remittances while productivity stayed low, and income per person reached its highest level yet in 2025.

threads.title: Remittances carry the economy
threads.text: After Hurricane Mitch in 1998, Hondurans began moving to the United States in large numbers, and the money they send home has become the main engine of spending. The World Bank describes growth over the last decade as driven largely by consumption paid for by remittances.

threads.title: Storms, droughts and El Niño
threads.text: Hurricane Mitch in 1998 ended a period of expansion. In 2020 hurricanes Eta and Iota struck with a force like Mitch's, and together with the pandemic they brought the deepest fall in the record. Droughts that come with El Niño weigh on farming and on the power made by dams, and an El Niño drought was expected to do so again in 2026.

threads.text: In 2009 the global financial crisis arrived together with a political crisis at home, and income per person fell 4.5 percent. The World Bank says the gains against poverty made in the mid-2000s were wiped out, and the political divisions of that year lingered for years after.

threads.text: The sources describe growth that rests on household spending more than on workers producing more. Most workers hold informal service jobs, and productivity has stayed low.

since_last_year.text: In 2025 record coffee prices and a surge in remittances lifted growth, and income per person reached a new high. A new government took office in January 2026 after close elections in November 2025. Through 2026 higher oil prices, slower remittances and an El Niño drought were expected to slow growth, and Congress approved a reform of the electricity sector in September 2026.

growth_story.tension: The data show income per person rising 17.7 percent a year from 1990 to 1997, but no source describes a boom of that size: the World Bank speaks only of a period of expansion that Hurricane Mitch ended in 1998, while the data show 1998 and 1999 as strong years, at 8.7 percent each. More recently, the World Bank reports solid GDP growth over 2015–2025, yet income per person grew only 1.6 percent a year over 2016–2025, so a growing population took up much of the gain.
